newsitem.title: UK: BAA unveils Heathrow Express, customer target.
newsitem.headline: BAA unveils Heathrow Express, customer target.

text.p: British airport operator BAA Plc unveiled the first of its 100 miles-per-hour Heathrow Express trains on Monday and said it planned to take 6 million passengers in its first year from rival taxi, coach and London Underground operators.
The new train fleet is part of a major 440 million pounds ($728 million) BAA investment in a high-speed rail link from London's Paddington station to Europe's biggest airport hub.
Predicting the impact of the Express trains, Sir John Egan, BAA chief executive, said "We anticipate taking 3,000 cars off the roads daily," once the service begins in June 1998.
Rod Hoare, chairman of the Heathrow Express service and BAA director of rail strategy told Reuters he aimed to take up to six million passengers in the first full year of operating..

At present around 54 million passengers travel through Heathrow airport, 28 percent of which is transfer traffic to another airport. The remainder -- travelling to and from Heathrow - is BAA's target market.
"We plan to pick up 15 percent of that market -- but actually I think we'll do even better than that," said Hoare.

The Heathrow Express rail service plans to carve out market share from the taxi, coach and London Underground operators, offering a 15 minute service from Paddington station in west London to Heathrow.
BAA revealed its forecast fare was 10 pounds one way, with a return fare possibly pitching in at 20 pounds.
The full rail service does not begin until next year. From this autumn onwards, however, BAA will run an interim 30 minute coach and rail service to Heathrow -- dubbed the FastTrain service.
Of the 440 million pounds BAA investment, just over 70 million pounds was paid to Siemens for the specially designed silver and blue rolling stock and for a 10 year maintenance contract.

Phil Tizzard, group managing director of Siemens Plc, the British arm of Germany's Siemens AG, added that this type of deal was "a sign of the times --that manufacturers now take on responsibility for ensuring the trains are available for service."

Jurgen Gehrels, chief executive of Siemens Plc, said at the unveiling of the train amid strobe lights and dry ice, "the objective given to us when we were bidding for this contract was that it should be an extension of the airline experience."
Out of the 70 million payment to Siemens, the rolling stock contract was 50 million, with the remainder for maintenance.

The bulk of the remaining BAA investment has gone on infrastructure, said Egan. "Most of the remaining investment here has gone on tunnelling, electrification of lines and upgrades at Paddington," he told Reuters.
Siemens hopes for further business from BAA's plans to try and provide a similar fast-link service to Heathrow from St Pancras station in central London.
Talks are currently underway with Railtrack Plc, the rail infrastructure group, about upgrading track to take the fast trains.
In future BAA would like to see through ticketing, allowing air passengers to use a single ticket covering the train journey to Heathrow and their final airline destination.

"The technology to provide a ticket for Paddington to Heathrow to Chicago and back could be done within a year. Certainly by the time we open our full service next year. We are talking to the airlines at the moment," said BAA's Hoare. ($ = 0.604 British Pounds)
